title: The house filled with fragrance (John 12:1–11)
hookLine: Mary anoints his feet and wipes them with her hair
tomorrow: unless a grain of wheat falls

cards: One breath of a certain soap, a certain bread, a certain perfume, and you can be seven years old again, or standing next to someone you lost.
Six days before Passover, Jesus comes back to Bethany, to the house of the friends he loves. They give him a dinner. Martha serves, of course.
Lazarus, dead and buried not long ago, is sitting at the table, eating. And then Mary gets up, carrying something.

teach.b: "Then took Mary a pound of ointment of spikenard, very costly, and anointed the feet of Jesus, and wiped his feet with her hair: and the house was filled with the odour of the ointment."

Spikenard, or nard, is an oil from a plant that grows high in the Himalayas. It had to travel thousands of miles to reach a village in Judea. A Roman pound is about twelve ounces, a great deal of perfume.
Honored guests were sometimes anointed on the head.
Mary goes to his feet, and wipes them with her hair. A woman letting down her hair in front of guests was a striking thing in that world. She doesn't seem to care.

And the whole house smells of it; John is the Gospel writer who notices that. Judas objects, and his question sounds reasonable: "Why was not this ointment sold for three hundred pence, and given to the poor?"

Three hundred denarii, about a year's wages for a laborer. John adds that Judas kept the money bag and helped himself from it. Jesus answers: "Let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this."
Mary is anointing a body for burial while it's still alive. She seems to understand what's coming better than anyone at the table. One more detail.

teach.h: THE HOUSE WAS FILLED WITH THE ODOR.
teach.b: Christians in the West have sometimes blended this Mary with Mary Magdalene and with an unnamed woman in Luke's Gospel.
Eastern churches kept them separate, and since its 1969 reform the Catholic calendar treats them as different women. John simply calls her Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus.

how: Christians read Mary's anointing in Holy Week in many churches; in some traditions, fragrant oil is used to anoint at baptism, confirmation and healing.

o: a cheap olive oil used for everyday cooking
a costly perfumed oil from a faraway mountain plant
a sweet wine poured out at the Passover meal

games.q: what's inside John 12:1–11 — tap the pairs.
p: against the day of my burying
why Mary kept it, Jesus says

s: Mary anointed Jesus's head in John's account
in John, she anoints his feet and wipes them with her hair.
Judas said the ointment should be sold for the poor
and John adds that he kept the money bag and stole from it.
in John, this Mary is Mary Magdalene
John calls her Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus. Eastern churches kept them separate.

games.q: you're at the dinner. Mary has just poured a year's wages of perfume on Jesus's feet. Judas complains. what does Jesus say?
o: "let her alone: she kept this for my burial."
games.why: "let her alone: against the day of my burying hath she kept this." she understands what's coming.

practice: If something with a scent is near you, soap, a spice, a flower, coffee, lotion, bring it close, or remember one, and breathe in slowly through your nose, noticing what it brings back, or who.
Then think of someone you love, and imagine giving them something extravagant, not useful, just beautiful, because they matter.
If you pray, offer this moment to God as Mary offered the nard; if not, simply breathe in the scent with gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Nard. The costly oil, also called spikenard, that Mary poured on Jesus's feet, until the whole house smelled of it.

orig.note: Greek: nard, spikenard. A rare oil from a plant of the Himalayas.

carryVoice: Your line: the house was filled. All from one costly jar, poured out. Day six hundred twenty-five, done.
